extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, designers, patrons, critics, and educated readers interested in principles of art and craftsmanship
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles for judging and producing architectural and artisanal work (especially Gothic): what qualities to seek or avoid in design, execution, labor practices, and patronage. Emphasis on the moral and aesthetic consequences of finish, invention, division of labour, and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servile ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Servile ornament, in which the execution or power of the inferior workman is entirely subjected to the intellect of the higher.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal schools: Greek, Ninevite, Egyptian. Greek servility: master gives only geometrical forms executable with absolute precision so the inferior workman cannot err. Assyrian/Egyptian: inferior workman allowed subjects he can only execute imperfectly but a legal standard for that imperfection is fixed by discipline. Result: the workman is a slave; look for absolute uniformity and rule-bound repetition as signs of servile ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Constitutional ornament, in which the executive inferior power is, to a certain point, emancipated and independent, having a will of its own, yet confessing its inferiority and rendering obedience to higher powers.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediate system where subordinate workmen have some independence of execution but still acknowledge the guiding authority of higher design. Expect some variety in execution but remaining deference to overall design principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Revolutionary ornament, in which no executive inferiority is admitted at all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System in which subordinate execution is fully self-determining (no admitted inferiority). Implies maximal freedom for the craftsman and a potential for perpetual novelty and individual expression in each piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savageness / rudeness as a noble character
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘savageness of Gothic architecture…may be considered, in some sort, a noble character,’ both as expression of northern origin and as an index of religious principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roughness of work, wildness of thought, and ungainly shapes are not reproach but dignity; they reflect a different climate, mode of life, and spiritual condition and should be recognized as essential qualities rather than faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit and value imperfection (Christian principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity 'recognizes, in small things as well as great, the individual value of every soul' and 'confesses its imperfection,' bestowing dignity upon the acknowledgment of unworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept results from inferior minds, and out of imperfect fragments raise a stately whole. The architect/artist should receive imperfect contributions indulgently and allow them to contribute to the whole rather than suppressing them for the sake of uniform perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize invention over finish
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Always look for invention first, and after that, for such execution as will help the invention, and as the inventor is capable of without painful effort, and no more.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek originality and thought before demanding technical polish. Finish is desirable when it serves the invention and is within the inventor's natural capacity; do not value finish above the underlying idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand exact finish for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Never demand an exact finish for its own sake, but only for some practical or noble end.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse to prize mere surface perfection where it adds nothing to meaning or utility. Examples: trivial exactness (sandpapered finish) is slave's work; finish is justifiable when it furthers a noble purpose or practical need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manufacture of unnecessary, uninventive articles
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Never encourage the manufacture of any article not absolutely necessary, in the production of which Invention has no share.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patronage of purely repetitive, thoughtless products (example: glass beads produced by rote processes) perpetuates degrading labour. Prefer to spend on objects where invention, design, or noble purpose are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not encourage imitation or copying except to preserve records
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Never encourage imitation or copying of any kind, except for the sake of preserving record of great works.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation fosters manufacture rather than art; copying is only defensible as archival preservation of exemplary works, not as a mode of creative production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not unhumanize workers—either make a tool or a man
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘You must either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him. You cannot make both.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you demand tool-like precision (cogs and compasses) you must sacrifice the worker's humanity; if you enable the worker to think, you will accept roughness and error but gain the worker's dignity and creative capacity. Policies and patron choices should avoid converting workers into merely precise instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour must not fragment human beings
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern division of labour often 'divides the men:--Divided into mere segments of men' so that a worker only produces a tiny repetitive part (a pin-point) rather than a whole product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such fragmentation degrades human beings and produces everything except formed human spirits. Remedy by valuing and demanding products of healthy, ennobling labour and by structuring work so individuals can exercise a range of faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changefulness / Variety as an essential mental element
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘CHANGEFULNESS, or Variety’ is named as the second mental element of Gothic; great art ‘does not say the same thing over and over again’ and should be 'capable of perpetual novelty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design forms (e.g., pointed arches, grouped shafts) should admit infinite variation. Variety is central to human delight in art; monotony indicates manufacture, not genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure workmen’s freedom by variety of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The degree in which the workman is degraded may be thus known at a glance, by observing whether the several parts of the building are similar or not.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If capitals, mouldings, or other parts are identical, the workman is enslaved; perpetual change in design and execution indicates that the workman was set free. Use sameness vs variety as a diagnostic for the social and artistic quality of a building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for perfection is a misunderstanding of art’s ends
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The demand for perfection is always a sign of a misunderstanding of the ends of art.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great artists' minds outrun their powers and will produce imperfections; striving for mechanical perfection often ruins life and expression. Expect and accept imperfection as inherent to great human work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection is a sign of life and a source of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfection is 'in some sort essential to all that we know of life'—irregularities and deficiencies are signs of vitality and sources of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry and rule-bound completeness remove expression and effort; irregularity is natural and desirable (examples: unequal leaves, asymmetrical faces). To banish imperfection is to paralyse vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patrons must choose between form (invention) and finish
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If the workman is thinking about his edges, he cannot be thinking of his design… Choose whether you will pay for the lovely form or the perfect finish…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that in many crafts one cannot have both highest invention and highest mechanical finish from the same hand. Patrons should deliberately allocate resources toward either inventive form or exact finish, not expect both for nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masters should practice manual work; all professions should be liberal
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The painter should grind his own colours; the architect work in the mason's yard with his men; the master-manufacturer be himself a more skilful operative than any man in his mills.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders in arts and trades ought not to disdain manual tasks—practical engagement keeps thought healthy and prevents the social division that produces morbid thinkers and miserable workers. Encourage hands-on competence among masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is not manufacture—avoid slavish rule-following
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Exactly so far as architecture works on known rules, and from given models, it is not an art, but a manufacture.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where work is produced merely by copying canonical forms and obeying fixed models (e.g., unvarying orders or capitals), it forfeits the character of art. True art invents and varies; do not mistake technical correctness for artistic merit.
